newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes down in US, hurt by ex-Treasury head.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes down in US, hurt by ex-Treasury head.

text.p: *Dlr/yen down but above 112.90 low. Treasury's Rubin supports strong dollar after early Bentsen remark knocks below 113. *Dealers see good appetite for dollar/yen at lows, Japan public fund rumored bidding for dollars on way down. *Dlr/mark, Swiss lose ground after early long liquidation. *U.S. assets turn down, hurting dollar, despite good jobs data.
The dollar closed lower against most leading currencies after former United States Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen said a stronger dollar could harm U.S. exporters.
Bentsen, in an interview with Reuters Financial Television, said he was "comfortable" with the dollar's current strong exchange rate.

But, referring to the dollar's value against the yen, he added: "If it continues to rise and goes substantially above this, of course, it puts us at a competitive disadvantage. I would prefer not to see it increase in value."

After briefly trading below the important 113 yen threshold, the dollar recovered somewhat when Robert Rubin, the administration's current Treasury chief told reporters at a press conference "we believe in a strong dollar."

"Bentsen's comment pushed it lower but then Treasury Secretary Rubin made a comment which took the dollar back up," said Kisoo Park, senior foreign exchange dealer at Bank of Boston. "I would presume Rubin carries more weight."
The dollar ended at 113.35/45 yen on Friday, down from 113.67/70 yen at the open and at 1.5135/45 marks, off from 1.5185/90 marks.
Bentsen served as Treasury Secretary for the first two years of the Clinton Administration.
During his tenure at the Treasury, many currency traders thought he favored an informal cap on dollar/yen around 113.
Bentsen gave some the impression of adhering to a policy of benign neglect of the dollar, believing a weaker U.S. currency would force trade concessions from Japan and spur sales of U.S. goods there.
But while traders said Bentsen's remarks may have a fleeting impact on the market, they come amid a recent chorus of complaints about the dollar's strength.

"The only thing it does signal is that there is still a body of opinion in the United States that does think the dollar is too strong at the moment," said Chris Iggo, an international economist at BZW/Barclays Bank in New York.

Many large U.S. coroporations, particularly the three largest U.S. auto manufacturers, have recently voiced concern over the damage a strong dollar could inflict on foreign demand for U.S. made goods.

The dollar was lifted earlier against the mark and extended its recent advance against the Swiss franc to a 20-month high at 1.2778 Swiss after a tame report on U.S. payroll growth briefly hoisted the U.S. bond market.

The Labor Department showed that the unemployment rate remained steady at 5.2 percent, while non-farm payrolls increased 210,000 in October, after falling 35,000 in September. The data was very close to Wall Street forecasts.
"The dollar got a slight boost from the bonds, but I don't think the bonds turning (lower) made the dollar go down," said Mark Remigio, a vice president at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.

The dollar could not hang on to gains versus the mark, which firmed in Asian trade after a German central banker, speaking in Singapore, said there was no need for a mark-damaging reduction in German interest rates.
The dollar fell to 1.2690/00 Swiss francs from 1.2715/25 and to Canadian $1.3335/40 from C$1.3366/71.
The pound touched $1.6445, its highest level since March 1995, but closed at $1.6360/70, off from $1.6373/80.
The Australian dollar stood a $0.7889/94, up from $0.7883/88 at the open.
-- Alden Bentley 212 859 1667
